Response to a single training session

Source: R/banister-responses.R
session_response.Rd

Computes the effect on predicted performance of one unit of load on the days after a single session (the influence curve), the time until that effect becomes positive and the time until it is largest (MODELS.md, M-05). Nothing is fitted: the parameters are given by the user.

Usage

session_response(
  k1,
  tau1,
  k2 = NULL,
  tau2 = NULL,
  model = c("two_component", "fitness_only"),
  days = 60,
  same_day_load = c("exclude", "include")
)

Arguments

k1

Gain of fitness, a single finite number >= 0.

tau1

Time constant of fitness in days, a single finite number > 0. Arguments are time constants, never half-lives (D-024): see time_constant() to convert a half-life.

k2

Gain of fatigue, a single finite number >= 0. Required for the two-component model; must not be given for the fitness-only model.

tau2

Time constant of fatigue in days, a single finite number > 0. Required for the two-component model; must not be given for the fitness-only model.

model

"two_component" (the default; fitness and fatigue) or "fitness_only" (D-023).

days

Last day of the curve, a single whole number >= 1. The curve runs from day 0 (the day of the session) to days.

same_day_load

Timing convention: "exclude" (the default) or "include". See the section on the timing convention.

Value

A list of class "session_response" with the elements

  • curve: a data frame with the columns day (0 to days) and effect (effect on predicted performance per unit of load);

  • time_to_recover, time_to_peak (days) and peak_effect (per unit of load), each a number or NA;

  • model, same_day_load, days and parameters: the arguments used.

Formula

The effect \(u\) days after one unit of load is $$L(u) = k_1\,e^{-u/\tau_1} - k_2\,e^{-u/\tau_2}$$ for the two-component model, and \(k_1\,e^{-u/\tau_1}\) for the fitness-only model. For \(\tau_1 > \tau_2\), $$\mathrm{time\_to\_recover} = \frac{\tau_1 \tau_2}{\tau_1 - \tau_2} \ln\frac{k_2}{k_1}, \qquad \mathrm{time\_to\_peak} = \frac{\tau_1 \tau_2}{\tau_1 - \tau_2} \ln\frac{k_2 \tau_1}{k_1 \tau_2},$$ and peak_effect is \(L\) at time_to_peak. These are \(t_n\) and \(t_g\) of Clarke & Skiba (2013) and Busso & Chalencon (2023); they are named in words because Morton et al. (1990) use \(t_n\) for a different quantity, the time_of_minimum of constant_training() (DECISIONS.md, D-026).

Timing convention

The times do not depend on the convention. Only the effect on the day of the session (day 0 of curve) does: \(k_1 - k_2\) with same_day_load = "include", 0 with "exclude" (the default, D-012). From day 1 on, both conventions give \(L(u)\).

When the times are NA

The times are NA when they do not exist (D-026):

  • time_to_recover is NA when \(k_2 \le k_1\): the effect is positive from the first day after the session, so there is nothing to recover from.

  • time_to_peak and peak_effect are NA when \(k_2 \tau_1 \le k_1 \tau_2\): the effect is largest right after the session and only decreases.

  • Both are NA when \(k_1 = 0\) (the effect is never positive), when \(\tau_1 \le \tau_2\) (fatigue does not fade faster than fitness), and for the fitness-only model (there is no fatigue).

References

Clarke DC, Skiba PF (2013). Rationale and resources for teaching the mathematical modeling of athletic training and performance. Advances in Physiology Education, 37, 134-152.

Busso T, Chalencon S (2023). Validity and accuracy of impulse-response models for modeling and predicting training effects on performance of swimmers. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise, 55(7), 1274-1285.

Ceddia D, Bondell H, Taylor P (2025). Mathematical modelling and optimisation of athletic performance: tapering and periodisation. arXiv:2505.20859 (preprint).

See also

simulate_banister(), constant_training(), half_life().

Examples

# Parameters of Morton et al. (1990)
r <- session_response(k1 = 1, tau1 = 45, k2 = 2, tau2 = 15)
r
#> <session_response> Response to a single session: two-component model
#> Timing convention: same_day_load = "exclude" (a day's load affects performance from the next day)
#> Parameters: k1 = 1, k2 = 2
#> Time constants: tau1 = 45 days (half-life 31.19 days), tau2 = 15 days (half-life 10.4 days)
#> Time to recover: 15.6 days
#> Time to peak: 40.31 days (effect 0.2722 per unit of load)
#> Curve: days 0 to 60 in $curve; day 0 is the day of the session.
head(r$curve)
#>   day     effect
#> 1   0  0.0000000
#> 2   1 -0.8929911
#> 3   2 -0.7938179
#> 4   3 -0.7019545
#> 5   4 -0.6169094
#> 6   5 -0.5382233

# Fit of Clarke & Skiba (2013)
session_response(k1 = 0.18258, tau1 = 35.821, k2 = 0.23016, tau2 = 21.340)
#> <session_response> Response to a single session: two-component model
#> Timing convention: same_day_load = "exclude" (a day's load affects performance from the next day)
#> Parameters: k1 = 0.1826, k2 = 0.2302
#> Time constants: tau1 = 35.82 days (half-life 24.83 days), tau2 = 21.34 days (half-life 14.79 days)
#> Time to recover: 12.22 days
#> Time to peak: 39.57 days (effect 0.02446 per unit of load)
#> Curve: days 0 to 60 in $curve; day 0 is the day of the session.
